claims.text: As-solidified HfNbTaTiZr has a heterogeneous microstructure containing coexisting domains or phases.
The coexisting domains or phases have different thermal expansion coefficients.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the domains generates local residual stress fields during cooling and thermal cycling.
Residual thermal stresses are the governing cause of the alloy's unusual stress-strain and thermoelastic behavior.
Residual stresses alter high-temperature mechanical behavior by changing dislocation dynamics.
Residual stresses facilitate dislocation motion during creep at 1250 °C.
Residual stresses facilitate dynamic recovery during creep at 1250 °C.
Residual stresses modify the alloy's effective elastic response.
A modified heat treatment or minor alloying adjustment can reduce microstructural heterogeneity and thermal-expansion mismatch.
Reducing thermal-expansion mismatch will lower residual stresses relative to conventionally processed HfNbTaTiZr.
Lower residual stresses will produce slower tensile-creep rates at 1250 °C.
Lower residual stresses will make elastic moduli vary less between 293 and 1100 K.
Lower residual stresses will produce a more subdued hardening response after aging at 600–800 °C.
The conventionally processed baseline has significant thermal-expansion mismatch.
Phase segregation is a plausible competing microstructural influence on mechanical behavior.
High-temperature oxidation is a plausible competing influence on high-temperature mechanical behavior.
Residual stress, creep rate, elastic modulus, and hardness will be compared between a standard batch and a modified batch over the stated temperature ranges.

contradictions.description: The design proposes a minor alloying adjustment while also requiring all other variables to remain constant; changing alloy composition is itself a major changed variable and would not isolate thermal-expansion mismatch from chemistry-dependent phase and dislocation effects.
